# Automated Tailored Text Messaging to Improve Blood Pressure in Community Health Centers: The TEXT-BP Randomized Clinical Trial

Daniel R. Okafor, MD, MPH; Priya Venkataraman, PhD; Maria Elena Castillo, RN, MSN; Thomas J. Brandt, MS; Aisha N. Whitfield, MD, MS

Division of General Internal Medicine, Northfield University School of Medicine, Lake Arden, Ohio (Okafor, Whitfield); Department of Biostatistics, Northfield University School of Public Health, Lake Arden, Ohio (Venkataraman, Brandt); Lakeshore Community Health Network, Lake Arden, Ohio (Castillo).

Corresponding Author: Daniel R. Okafor, MD, MPH, Division of General Internal Medicine, Northfield University School of Medicine, 400 Harbor View Rd, Lake Arden, Ohio (d.okafor@northfield-medicine.example).

Article type: Original Investigation. Exhibits: 3 tables, 2 figures. Supplements: trial protocol and statistical analysis plan (Supplement 1); CONSORT checklist (Supplement 2).

## Key Points

**Question:** Does a 12-month program of automated, tailored text messages lower systolic blood pressure among adults with uncontrolled hypertension who receive care in community health centers?

**Findings:** In this randomized clinical trial of 1,208 adults, systolic blood pressure decreased by 4.2 mm Hg more over 12 months with tailored text messaging than with attention-control messages, a statistically significant difference.

**Meaning:** Automated text messaging is a low-cost adjunct to usual care that modestly improved blood pressure in a safety-net population.

## Abstract

**Importance:** Uncontrolled hypertension is common among adults who receive care in community health centers, and poor medication adherence is a modifiable contributor. Whether low-cost automated text messaging improves blood pressure in this setting is uncertain.

**Objective:** To determine whether 12 months of automated, tailored text messages improves systolic blood pressure (SBP) compared with attention-control messages.

**Design, Setting, and Participants:** Parallel-group randomized clinical trial at 12 federally qualified community health centers in Ohio. Adults aged 18 to 80 years with office SBP of 140 mm Hg or higher taking at least 1 antihypertensive medication were enrolled from March 2022 to August 2023; final follow-up was in September 2024.

**Interventions:** Participants were randomized 1:1 to tailored text messaging (adherence reminders, education, and 2-way refill prompts; n = 604) or attention-control messages (monthly general health messages; n = 604), each added to usual care.

**Main Outcomes and Measures:** The prespecified primary outcome was change in office SBP from baseline to 12 months, measured by masked assessors. Secondary outcomes included blood pressure (BP) control (<140/90 mm Hg), pharmacy refill adherence (proportion of days covered ≥80%), change in diastolic BP, and adverse events.

**Results:** Among 1,208 randomized participants (mean [SD] age, 58.4 [11.2] years; 652 [54.0%] women), 1,100 (91.1%) completed the 12-month visit. Mean SBP decreased by 11.8 mm Hg with text messaging and by 7.6 mm Hg with attention control (adjusted difference in SBP change, −4.2 mm Hg [95% CI, −6.1 to −2.3]; P < .001). BP control was achieved by 50.1% vs 41.3% of participants (risk difference, 8.8 percentage points [95% CI, 3.0 to 14.6]), and refill adherence was 68.4% vs 55.9% (risk difference, 12.5 percentage points [95% CI, 7.1 to 17.9]). Serious adverse events occurred in 38 (6.3%) and 41 (6.8%) participants, respectively.

**Conclusions and Relevance:** Among adults with uncontrolled hypertension in community health centers, automated tailored text messaging produced a modest reduction in SBP at 12 months compared with attention control. Its durability and effect on cardiovascular events remain unknown.

**Trial Registration:** ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT09000017

## 1. Introduction

Hypertension is the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease and death worldwide (Mills et al., 2020). Each 10 mm Hg reduction in systolic blood pressure (SBP) lowers the risk of major cardiovascular events by roughly one-fifth (Ettehad et al., 2016), and current US guidelines recommend a treatment target below 130/80 mm Hg for most adults (Whelton et al., 2018). Yet blood pressure control in the United States has stagnated over the past decade, and control rates are lowest among patients with low income, limited English proficiency, and Black or Hispanic race and ethnicity, the populations served disproportionately by federally qualified community health centers.

Suboptimal adherence to prescribed antihypertensive medication is a common and modifiable reason for uncontrolled blood pressure (Burnier and Egan, 2019). Adherence interventions that rely on clinician time, such as pharmacist visits or nurse case management, are effective but difficult to sustain in resource-constrained clinics. Short message service (SMS) text messaging is inexpensive, reaches patients without smartphones or data plans, and can be automated. A meta-analysis of 16 randomized trials found that text messaging approximately doubled the odds of medication adherence in chronic disease (Thakkar et al., 2016), but most included trials were short, measured adherence by self-report, and did not assess blood pressure as the primary outcome. Two influential trials suggest the approach can lower blood pressure: in a trial among patients with coronary heart disease in Australia, lifestyle-focused messages reduced SBP (Chow et al., 2015), and in a trial in South Africa, adherence messages produced a small reduction in SBP among adults with hypertension (Bobrow et al., 2016). Whether these findings extend to US safety-net clinics, where patients face cost, transportation, and language barriers, is unknown.

We therefore conducted the TEXT-BP trial to test whether 12 months of automated, tailored, bilingual text messaging, added to usual care, lowers SBP more than attention-control messages among adults with uncontrolled hypertension receiving care in community health centers.

## 2. Methods

### Trial Design

TEXT-BP was a parallel-group, 2-group randomized clinical trial with 1:1 allocation conducted at 12 federally qualified community health centers operated by the Lakeshore Community Health Network in northeast Ohio. The trial protocol and statistical analysis plan (Supplement 1) were finalized before enrollment, and no changes were made to eligibility criteria or outcomes after the trial began. This report follows the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) guideline (Schulz et al., 2010).

### Participants

Patients were eligible if they were aged 18 to 80 years, had a diagnosis of hypertension, had been prescribed at least 1 antihypertensive medication for at least 3 months, had a mean office SBP of 140 mm Hg or higher at a screening visit, owned a mobile telephone able to receive text messages, and could read English or Spanish. Exclusion criteria were SBP of 180 mm Hg or higher or diastolic blood pressure (DBP) of 110 mm Hg or higher at screening (referred for same-day care), estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30 mL/min/1.73 m², pregnancy, planned relocation within 12 months, enrollment in another blood pressure study, and inability to provide informed consent. Potentially eligible patients were identified from electronic health record registries and invited by letter and telephone; interested patients attended an in-person screening visit.

### Randomization and Masking

After the baseline visit, participants were randomized 1:1 using a computer-generated sequence with permuted blocks of 4 and 6, stratified by health center and baseline SBP (<160 vs ≥160 mm Hg). The sequence was generated by a statistician with no participant contact and was concealed in the randomization module of the study database; study data were collected in REDCap (Harris et al., 2009). Because of the nature of the intervention, participants and their clinicians were not masked to group assignment. Statisticians conducted the primary analysis with group labels masked.

### Outcome Assessment

Blood pressure at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months was measured by trained research assistants who were not involved in recruitment or intervention delivery and who were masked to group assignment; participants were asked not to disclose their messages. Measurements followed the American Heart Association scientific statement (Muntner et al., 2019): after 5 minutes of seated rest, 3 readings were obtained 1 minute apart with a validated automated oscillometric device and an appropriately sized cuff, and the mean of the second and third readings was recorded. Assessors were retrained and observed every 6 months.

### Interventions

Participants in the intervention group received automated text messages for 12 months in English or Spanish. The program comprised 3 components: (1) daily medication reminders timed to each participant's reported dosing schedule for the first 3 months, then tapering to 4 days per week; (2) 2 to 3 weekly educational messages on hypertension, home monitoring, sodium intake, and adverse effects, tailored to responses to a baseline questionnaire on adherence barriers; and (3) 2-way refill prompts sent 5 days before each expected refill date, to which participants could reply to request a refill or report a problem. Replies that indicated a problem (such as cost or adverse effects) generated a task for the health center's nurse care coordinator. Message content was developed with patient advisors from the participating health centers and pretested for readability at a sixth-grade level.

Participants in the attention-control group received 1 general health message per month (for example, on influenza vaccination or physical activity) with no content about blood pressure or medication. Both groups continued usual care, including routine visits, and clinicians in both groups could intensify treatment at their discretion. Participants received a $25 gift card at each study visit.

Message delivery was logged automatically by the messaging platform. A research coordinator reviewed delivery failures, opt-outs, and the time from each flagged reply to a care coordinator response every week; the prespecified fidelity target was a response within 2 business days for at least 90% of flagged replies. Participants who changed telephone numbers were re-enrolled in the platform at their next contact with the health center.

### Outcomes

The prespecified primary outcome, unchanged from the registered protocol, was the change in office SBP from baseline to 12 months. Prespecified secondary outcomes were change in office DBP at 12 months; change in SBP at 6 months; BP control, defined as office blood pressure below 140/90 mm Hg at 12 months; medication adherence, defined as a proportion of days covered of 80% or higher for antihypertensive medications during the 12-month follow-up, calculated from pharmacy dispensing records; and treatment intensification, defined as addition of a drug class or a dose increase recorded in the health record. Safety outcomes were serious adverse events, symptomatic hypotension, syncope, falls with injury, hyperkalemia or acute kidney injury, and emergency department visits, ascertained by participant report at each visit and by health record review by a clinician masked to group assignment.

### Sample Size

We assumed a standard deviation of 16 mm Hg for the 12-month change in SBP, based on prior community-based trials. A sample of 511 participants per group provides 85% power to detect a between-group difference of 3 mm Hg with a 2-sided α of .05. Allowing for 15% loss to follow-up, we planned to randomize 1,202 participants.

### Statistical Analysis

The primary analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle and included all 1,208 randomized participants in the group to which they were assigned, regardless of the number of messages received or opt-out. The 12-month change in SBP was compared between groups with linear regression adjusted for the stratification factors (health center and baseline SBP stratum) and baseline SBP, with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Missing 12-month values were handled with multiple imputation by chained equations under a missing-at-random assumption, using 20 imputed data sets that included baseline characteristics, 6-month blood pressure, and adherence, with estimates combined by Rubin's rules (Rubin, 1987; White et al., 2011).

Prespecified sensitivity analyses for the primary outcome were a complete-case analysis; a mixed model for repeated measures using both follow-up visits; a delta-adjusted tipping-point analysis in which imputed values in the intervention group were made progressively worse to assess departures from the missing-at-random assumption; and a per-protocol analysis restricted to participants who did not opt out and attended the 12-month visit. Binary secondary outcomes were analyzed as risk differences from linear probability models with the same covariates and robust standard errors. Heterogeneity of the treatment effect was assessed for 7 prespecified subgroups by testing a treatment-by-subgroup interaction term (Pocock et al., 2002).

The primary outcome was tested at a 2-sided α of .05. Because no adjustment was made for multiple comparisons, findings for secondary outcomes and subgroups should be interpreted as exploratory. Analyses were performed with R version 4.3.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing).

### Trial Oversight and Ethics

The trial was approved by the Northfield University institutional review board and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent in English or Spanish. An independent data and safety monitoring board reviewed enrollment, retention, and adverse events every 6 months; no interim efficacy analysis was planned or performed.

## 3. Results

### Participants

Of 2,946 patients screened, 1,738 were excluded (1,214 did not meet eligibility criteria, 431 declined, and 93 for other reasons), and 1,208 were randomized: 604 to text messaging and 604 to attention control (Figure 1). Enrollment occurred from March 2022 to August 2023, and the last 12-month visit occurred in September 2024. The 12-month primary outcome was measured in 1,100 participants (91.1%): 551 in the text-messaging group and 549 in the attention-control group. All 1,208 randomized participants were included in the primary analysis.

Baseline characteristics were similar between groups (Table 1). The mean (SD) age was 58.4 (11.2) years, 652 participants (54.0%) were women, 477 (39.5%) were Black, 272 (22.5%) were Hispanic, and 199 (16.5%) preferred Spanish. The mean (SD) baseline office blood pressure was 152.6 (11.8)/89.1 (10.6) mm Hg.

During follow-up, intervention participants received a median of 418 messages (IQR, 391-436), and 15 participants (2.5%) opted out of messaging. Participants replied to a median of 74% (IQR, 52%-88%) of refill prompts. Care coordinators responded to 1,184 of 1,262 flagged replies (93.8%) within 2 business days; the problems reported most often were medication cost (38.4% of flagged replies), running out of medication before a refill (27.1%), and adverse effects (14.6%).

### Primary Outcome

At 12 months, mean SBP had decreased by 11.8 mm Hg in the text-messaging group and by 7.6 mm Hg in the attention-control group (adjusted between-group difference, −4.2 mm Hg [95% CI, −6.1 to −2.3]; P < .001) (Table 2). Results were consistent in the complete-case analysis (−4.4 mm Hg [95% CI, −6.3 to −2.5]), the mixed model for repeated measures (−4.1 mm Hg [95% CI, −6.0 to −2.2]), and the per-protocol analysis (−4.6 mm Hg [95% CI, −6.6 to −2.6]). In the tipping-point analysis, the difference lost statistical significance only when missing outcomes in the intervention group were assumed to be 9.5 mm Hg worse than their imputed values.

The effect of text messaging on the primary outcome did not differ significantly across prespecified subgroups defined by age, sex, race and ethnicity, preferred language, baseline SBP, diabetes, and baseline adherence (all P for interaction ≥ .19) (Figure 2).

### Secondary Outcomes

Text messaging reduced DBP at 12 months (difference, −2.1 mm Hg [95% CI, −3.3 to −0.9]) and SBP at 6 months (difference, −3.3 mm Hg [95% CI, −5.0 to −1.6]) (Table 2). BP control at 12 months was achieved by 50.1% of participants in the text-messaging group and 41.3% in the attention-control group (risk difference, 8.8 percentage points [95% CI, 3.0 to 14.6]). The proportion with refill adherence of 80% or higher was 68.4% vs 55.9% (risk difference, 12.5 percentage points [95% CI, 7.1 to 17.9]). Treatment intensification was similar between groups (31.6% vs 29.8%; risk difference, 1.8 percentage points [95% CI, −3.4 to 7.0]).

### Adverse Events

Serious adverse events occurred in 38 participants (6.3%) in the text-messaging group and 41 (6.8%) in the attention-control group (Table 3). Symptomatic hypotension was reported by 13 participants (2.2%) and 11 participants (1.8%), respectively, and syncope by 3 (0.5%) and 2 (0.3%). No serious adverse event was judged by the data and safety monitoring board to be related to the intervention.

## 4. Discussion

In this randomized clinical trial among adults with uncontrolled hypertension receiving care in 12 community health centers, 12 months of automated, tailored text messaging reduced SBP by 4.2 mm Hg more than attention-control messages. The intervention also increased the proportion of participants with controlled blood pressure and with adequate refill adherence, without an increase in adverse events. The effect was evident at 6 months, persisted through 12 months, and was consistent across prespecified subgroups, including Spanish-speaking participants.

The magnitude of the effect is similar to that observed with lifestyle-focused messaging among patients with coronary heart disease (Chow et al., 2015) and larger than that observed with adherence messaging in South Africa (Bobrow et al., 2016). Several features may explain the difference from the latter trial: our messages were tailored to individual adherence barriers, the 2-way refill prompts were linked to a nurse care coordinator who could address cost and access problems, and the comparison group received messages that controlled for the attention of regular contact. The increase in pharmacy-measured adherence, together with similar rates of treatment intensification in the 2 groups, suggests that the blood pressure reduction operated mainly through improved adherence rather than through changes in prescribing, consistent with meta-analytic evidence (Thakkar et al., 2016).

A difference of 4.2 mm Hg is modest for an individual patient. At the population level, however, reductions of this size are associated with meaningful decreases in stroke and coronary events (Ettehad et al., 2016), and the program can be delivered at low marginal cost to every patient with a mobile telephone. Because the intervention required little clinician time beyond responding to flagged replies, it may be feasible in clinics that cannot staff pharmacist- or nurse-led programs. Text messaging should be regarded as a complement to, rather than a substitute for, timely treatment intensification, which remains the principal lever for reaching guideline targets (SPRINT Research Group, 2015; Whelton et al., 2018).

The findings also bear on implementation and equity. Community health centers already send text messages for appointment reminders, and the platform used in this trial drew on existing patient registries rather than on a separate application. The main incremental resource was care coordinator time for flagged replies, most of which were refill requests that could be routed directly to a pharmacy. That cost was the problem reported most often suggests that pairing messaging with access to low-cost generic medications may add to its effect. Estimates were similar among Spanish-speaking participants and across racial and ethnic groups, which suggests that a bilingual program written at a low reading level can reach the populations with the lowest rates of hypertension control. The trial was not powered to detect differences between subgroups, however, and subgroup estimates are imprecise.

### Limitations

This trial has limitations. First, participants and clinicians were aware of group assignment, although blood pressure was measured by masked assessors with an automated protocol, and the attention-control design reduces the influence of contact alone. Second, the 12-month follow-up cannot establish whether the effect persists after messaging stops or translates into fewer cardiovascular events. Third, 8.9% of participants did not complete the 12-month visit; results were robust to complete-case, repeated-measures, and tipping-point analyses, but outcomes that are missing not at random cannot be excluded. Fourth, adherence was measured by pharmacy dispensing, which captures medication possession rather than ingestion. Fifth, the trial was conducted in 1 health network in 1 state and required a mobile telephone and literacy in English or Spanish, which may limit generalizability to other settings and languages. Sixth, the trial was not designed to assess cost-effectiveness, which will be reported separately.

### Conclusions

In this randomized clinical trial among adults with uncontrolled hypertension receiving care in community health centers, automated tailored text messaging added to usual care modestly reduced SBP at 12 months compared with attention-control messages. Longer follow-up is needed to determine whether the effect is sustained and whether it reduces cardiovascular events.
